title: Pro-tip, if developing with godot, clone the entire open source engine code and tell Claude "You can reference the engine code at any time" - It improves claude performance 1000x.
author: _BreakingGood_
selftext: It regularly checks the engine code to figure out what is actually possible, which bypasses checking the documentation site that can be outdated or wrong.

replies.author: _BreakingGood_
replies.body:
It depends how it treats the github link. Sometimes it will try to actually browse the files on github by calling the website itself. Which heavily limits how far/wide it can explore the codebase versus having the entire thing on your local computer.

However, it's possible that if you just give it the github link, it will actually clone/download the source for you, and explore it there. If it does this approach, then yes it's the exact same as what im suggesting.

replies.author: loontoon
replies.body:
I'm not one-shotting anything. I've used more than 20 milion tokens in a month, with probably 1000 prompts, and almost 400 git commits across 18 branches.

I added tilt controls for tablets, mouse controls for desktop, lots of keyboard controls and I'm about to add controller support. None of the controls were a problem. 

But I do appreciate that different games have different requirements, so maybe your game has a more complicated control system. 

It just seems to me that Claude knows how to write GDscript extremely well even without an MCP

I asked Claude if it thought it would help and its response was "The core idea is sound; the "1000x" is Reddit talking. Here's my honest read on it.

**What's true:** I can't see inside the engine. When we hit questions like "does trimesh collision have backfaces?", "why doesn't a JS boolean survive `JavaScriptBridge.eval`?", or "what exactly does DirAccess return in a web export?", I'm working from documentation knowledge plus experiment. You've watched me answer those empirically — run the game, poke it, observe. With the engine source on disk I could sometimes grep the actual C++ and answer in one step instead of three, and with certainty instead of inference. It's genuinely useful for: undocumented behaviour, exact default values, import pipeline quirks (like the ufbx/GLB importer details), and "is this a bug in my code or the engine?" questions.

**What's oversold:** day-to-day work — GDScript, the node API, scene structure — I already know well, and having 1.5GB of C++ nearby changes nothing there. The clone isn't ambiently "loaded" into my head; it only helps when I deliberately go read it, which for most tasks I don't need to. Realistically it upgrades maybe one debugging session in ten from "experiment and infer" to "read the source and know." That's worth having. It's not a multiplier on everything.

**If we do it, two details matter:**

1. **Clone the tag matching your engine** — `4.6.3-stable` — not master, or the source I read could differ from the engine you run.
2. **Put it outside the game project** (e.g. `~/Dev/godot-source`). Inside the project, Godot would try to import thousands of engine files and my project-wide searches would drown in engine code.

It's a one-time shallow clone (\~a few hundred MB) plus a note in my memory so future sessions know it's there. Cheap insurance, occasional real payoff. Want me to set it up?"

  
Based on it's reply I've decided to copy the code, but I'm not expecting to see an huge difference in the output I'm already getting. 

Your mileage may vary.

replies.author: FjorgVanDerPlorg
replies.body:
Yeah I've literally got Claude Opus to find and write a shim plugin for a nasty memory leak (well actually 3 leaks), in the Niagara GeoCollection NDI. Thing basically orphans memory every frame, reported to Epic Games and known to exist in 5.6-5.8 (probably earlier ones too, I haven't looked).

The [plugin](https://github.com/MajorSmash/GeometryCollectionNDI-Fixed-) works, the memory leak isn't there when you use it. 100% vibe coded, I was curious how well it would do, but yeah it actually did find and fix a nasty engine bug.
